notes.b: Cooking methods fall into three groups according to what carries the heat to the food. The right choice depends on the food, the eater and the result you want.
points: Moist methods use water, stock or steam as the medium. Dry methods use hot air or radiant heat (heat given off as rays from a hot element or flame) with little or no added liquid. Fat-based methods use fat or oil as the medium.

The food: tender cuts and delicate foods such as fish, eggs and vegetables suit quick methods, because they need little time to become tender. Tough, fibrous cuts need long, moist methods, which soften the fibres.
Nutrition: steaming, stir-frying and grilling use little or no water and short times, so they conserve water-soluble vitamins. Boiling loses them into the cooking water unless that liquid is used.
Palatability (how pleasant the food is to eat): dry and fat-based methods brown and crisp the surface, adding colour and flavour, while moist methods give a soft, tender texture.
Diet: steaming, poaching, boiling and grilling on a rack add little or no fat, which suits a diet that limits fat. Deep-fat frying adds fat and energy because the food absorbs fat.
Consumer needs: an older person who has difficulty chewing or swallowing needs soft, moist, easily digested food, so a moist method is the better choice.
Time and equipment: a pressure cooker shortens cooking time, while stewing and braising are long, slow methods in a covered pan or oven.
Cost: slow moist cooking makes an inexpensive cut of meat tender and palatable, so you do not have to buy an expensive cut.
notes.tip: If you are asked to choose a method to conserve nutrients or lower fat, name the method and give the reason: for example, grilling lets fat drip away, and steaming uses no fat and keeps water-soluble vitamins.

notes.b: In moist methods the food is cooked in water, stock or steam. The temperature of the liquid is what separates them: boiling is hottest, simmering is just below it and poaching is lower again.
points: Boiling: food is cooked in rapidly bubbling water at boiling point, 100 °C at sea level. It is quick and used for vegetables, pasta, rice, eggs and potatoes, but water-soluble vitamins leach (dissolve) into the water.
Simmering: liquid is kept just below boiling point, with small bubbles breaking the surface. It is gentler than boiling and is used for stocks, soups, stews and stewed fruit.

Stewing: food is cooked slowly and gently in a small amount of liquid in a covered pan or casserole, on the hob or in the oven. It suits tough meat and vegetables, as in Irish stew, a traditional stew.
Stewing keeps nutrients because the liquid is served with the food.

Steaming: food is cooked by the steam from boiling water without touching the water, in a steamer, on a plate over a pan or in a covered bowl in a pan. No fat is added, and nutrients and shape are kept. It suits fish, chicken, vegetables, rice and steamed puddings.

Poaching: food is cooked gently in liquid kept slightly below simmering point, about 85 °C, on the hob or in the oven. It suits delicate foods that would break up or toughen in fiercer heat, such as eggs, fish and fruit like pears.
Braising: tough meat or vegetables are browned in fat, then cooked slowly with a little liquid in a covered dish, in the oven or on the hob. The long, slow, moist cooking tenderises tough cuts.

Pressure cooking: food is cooked in a sealed pan in which steam builds up pressure. This raises the temperature above 100 °C and shortens the cooking time. It is used for stocks, stews, tough meat and pulses.
notes.tip: Don't mix up the three liquid temperatures: poaching is below simmering, and simmering is below boiling. Examiners ask for a one-line definition of poaching, and for true or false on it: it suits delicate foods such as eggs and fish.

notes.b: Dry methods cook food with hot air or radiant heat rather than liquid. They brown the surface, which adds colour and flavour.
points: Roasting: meat, poultry, potatoes or vegetables are cooked uncovered in the oven in a roasting tin, usually with a little fat. The surface browns while the centre cooks by conduction and convection.

Baking: food is cooked by the dry heat of an oven, mainly by convection (hot air circulating) and radiation. It is used for cakes, bread, pastry, fish, pasta and potato dishes, as with fish pie and lasagne.

Grilling: food is cooked by radiant heat from an element or flame above or below it. The heat seals the surface, so it is a fast method. It suits tender cuts, steaks, chops, thin fish, sausages, rashers, tomatoes, mushrooms, peppers and kebabs.
Barbecuing: this is grilling outdoors on a grid over burning charcoal or gas, using radiant heat, which gives a smoky flavour.
Grilling lowers the fat content of food, because fat drips away from it.
notes.tip: Roasting is classed as dry in the marking schemes even though a little fat is used, so don't put it under fat-based methods. Grilling is a fast method; calling it slow is wrong.

notes.b: Grilling is fast and the heat is fierce, so food can burn outside while it is raw inside, or dry out. These rules prevent that.
points: Preheat the grill to the required temperature so that the surface seals on contact.
Oil the grid or the food to prevent sticking.
Use thin pieces, so that heat reaches the centre before the surface burns.
Do not add salt before grilling, because salt draws moisture to the surface.
Turn the food with tongs rather than a fork, so that its juices stay inside instead of running out through holes.
Use the correct cooking time, since grilled food dries out and overcooks quickly.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for three guidelines for grilling. Pick three and give the reason with each, such as preheating to seal the surface or tongs rather than a fork to keep the juices in.

notes.b: Fat-based methods, usually called frying, cook food in hot fat or oil. They give a crisp, golden surface, but the amount of fat used varies a great deal from one method to another.
points: Shallow frying: food is cooked in hot fat in a shallow pan, partly covered by the fat and turned once or twice, giving a crisp surface. It is used for eggs, fish, chops and pancakes.

Deep-fat frying: food is fully immersed in hot oil in a deep pan or fryer, which seals the surface quickly. It is used for chips and fish in batter. The food absorbs some fat, so it is higher in fat and energy than grilled food.
Stir-frying: small, thin pieces are tossed and stirred constantly over high heat in a wok or large pan with a little oil. Because the cooking is so quick, it keeps colour, crispness and vitamin C.
Dry frying: food is cooked in a non-stick pan without added fat, using the fat already in foods such as bacon rashers and sausages.
Pot roasting: meat is cooked in a little fat in a covered pan on the hob, so it cooks in its own juices and steam and stays moist. It is not done in the oven and not uncovered.
notes.tip: Define pot roasting as a covered pan on the hob with a little fat, and deep-fat frying as food immersed in hot fat. In both cases, say where and how the food is cooked.

notes.b: A microwave oven is a fast method that suits reheating and cooking small amounts. It works differently from the other methods, so its advantages and limits are worth knowing.
points: Microwave ovens cook and reheat quickly with little added fat and water, so vitamins are kept.
They do not brown food unless a grill or combination mode is used, so the surface stays pale.
Containers must be microwave-safe, and metal must not be used.

notes.h: Dishes and examples for each method
notes.b: Examiners often ask you to give dishes or foods for a method. These are the examples that are accepted.
points: Baking: apple crumble, sponge, soda bread, fish pie, lasagne, pizza and muffins.
Grilling: kebabs, chicken satay, burgers, fish, rashers, sausages, tomatoes, mushrooms and bruschetta.
Steaming: fish, chicken, rice, Christmas pudding (a traditional steamed pudding), fruit and vegetables. Roasting: meat, potatoes and vegetables.
Frying has four types: dry, shallow, deep and stir-fry. The moist methods are boiling, stewing, steaming, poaching, braising and pressure cooking.

Classifying methods: moist covers boiling, stewing, steaming, poaching, braising and pressure cooking. Dry covers baking, grilling, roasting and barbecuing. Frying covers dry, shallow, deep and stir-frying.
notes.tip: To classify methods, give moist, dry and frying with two examples each. True or false questions have asked that grilling is fast (true), that deep frying is cooking food immersed in hot fat (true) and that poaching suits delicate foods such as eggs and fish (true).

notes.b: Steaming is a good choice for an older person because it is simple and gives soft food that is easy to eat. It also has weaknesses, so a full evaluation covers ease, nutrition and palatability.
points: Ease: steaming needs little attention or equipment, a whole meal can cook in a tiered steamer, and it suits small portions.
Texture: the moist, soft food is easy to chew and swallow, which suits an older person with difficulty chewing or swallowing.
Nutrition: steaming adds no fat, so it suits a diet that limits fat. Because the food does not sit in water, water-soluble vitamins (B and C) are kept.
Palatability: steamed food keeps its colour and moisture, but it can taste bland and does not brown. Overcooking spoils its texture and colour.
Fish, chicken, rice and vegetables suit steaming; steamed puddings are a traditional example.
Herbs, lemon juice and a sauce add flavour without added salt, which suits a diet that limits salt.
notes.tip: When you evaluate steaming for an older person, refer to ease, nutritive value and palatability, and give both advantages and drawbacks. Finish with a conclusion.

keyTerms.definition: Methods that cook food in water, stock or steam, such as boiling, stewing, steaming and poaching.
Methods that cook food with hot air or radiant heat and little or no added liquid, such as roasting, baking and grilling.
Methods that use fat as the cooking medium, such as shallow frying, deep-fat frying and stir-frying.
Cooking food gently in liquid kept slightly below simmering point.
Slow cooking of food in a small amount of liquid in a covered pan.
Browning meat in fat, then cooking it slowly with a little liquid in a covered dish.
Cooking food in a little fat in a covered pan on the hob.
Cooking food in the steam from boiling water, without the food being immersed in the water.
Quick cooking of small pieces of food tossed in a little oil over high heat.
Cooking food by radiant heat from an element above or below it.

factCards.definition: Its soft, moist texture is easy to chew and swallow; it adds no fat; it retains nutrients and keeps its colour and moisture.
Food is cooked in a little fat in a covered pan on the hob, retaining its own juices.

questions.prompt: Name three foods suited to grilling and explain why grilling suits each of them.
questions.model: Any three of: fish, sausages, rashers, steak, lamb cutlets, tomatoes, mushrooms, peppers, fruit kebabs. Explanation for each: the radiant heat of the grill browns and cooks the surface quickly; foods that are thin or tender cook through before they dry out, since heat reaches the centre quickly in thin pieces and tender cuts have little connective tissue to soften; fat drips away, so the finished food is lower in fat. Full marks need a named food and a reason for each.

questions.prompt: A family is planning a meal with a tough cut of beef and a fillet of white fish. Describe a suitable moist cooking method for each food and explain how the method conserves nutrients and improves palatability. Then explain two factors a cook should consider when choosing between a dry and a moist method for a meal for an older person.
questions.model: Beef: braising or stewing, with the meat browned in fat, then cooked slowly with a little liquid in a covered dish; the long moist cooking converts collagen into gelatine, tenderising the meat and giving a rich, soft texture; the small amount of liquid and low temperature limit the loss of water-soluble vitamins, and the juices can be served as gravy. Fish: steaming or poaching; the fish cooks gently in steam or liquid just below simmering, so it stays moist, keeps its shape and flakes in tender pieces, and vitamins are retained because the food does not sit in boiling water. Two factors for an older person: the texture must be soft and moist, since dry methods such as roasting or grilling can make food hard to chew and swallow; the method should add little or no fat, since moist methods such as steaming add none; and the method should retain nutrients and flavour, which moist methods do by using little water and short cooking.
